screens.title: Caching: Principles, Strategies, and Eviction Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Caching is a simple idea with deep impact: keep frequently used data closer so requests cost less time and backend resources. In this chapter you will learn why caching reduces latency and backend load, the common places it’s applied—from the user's device to a database buffer pool—and the trade-offs that come with consistency and capacity limits. We will ground the ideas with concrete strategies you’ll see in interviews: write-through, write-back, and write-around, and we’ll step through popular eviction policies like LRU, LFU, and FIFO so you can justify design choices. You will also see common pitfalls engineers face: stale data causing incorrect user experience, cache stampedes that overwhelm origins, and over-caching that wastes memory and complicates invalidation. By the end, you’ll be able to describe when to cache, which layer to choose, how to invalidate safely, and how to reason about eviction under capacity constraints. Keep an eye on practical examples: an e-commerce inventory update, a CDN serving static assets, and an in-memory LRU used by an A P I. These examples will let you connect the principles to interview scenarios and real-world trade-offs. Ready to explore the three key areas: layers, invalidation strategies, and eviction policies?

screens.title: What is a Cache and Why It Helps
screens.narratorSegment: A cache is a temporary storage area that holds frequently accessed data so future requests can be served faster. The central claim is that by keeping a copy of hot data in a faster, closer store you reduce both latency and load on slower origins. Picture a busy library where the closet with seldom-used books is far away; placing the most commonly referenced books on a nearby desk is like caching. The immediate benefit is lower response time for reads and reduced queries to the origin database or remote A P I. That improves scalability: fewer expensive operations means your backend can serve more users. A concrete example is storing rendered user session data in an in-memory cache so page loads skip repeated database queries. A common misconception is that caches always give fresh data; they don’t—unless you design invalidation. Stale caches can return outdated information, and over-reliance on caching can mask correctness bugs. Key practical signals to watch are cache hit rate and the origin request rate. High hit rate with low origin traffic shows successful caching; low hit rate suggests wasted memory or poor key design. As a takeaway, always pair caching with a clear invalidation or TTL strategy and measure hit rates so you know whether the cache is actually helping. How would you measure success for a newly deployed cache in production?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is a Cache?
Cache — concise definition
Temporary fast storage for frequently accessed data to reduce subsequent access cost.
Analogy
Like keeping frequently used books on a desk rather than walking to the storage shed.
Why it matters
  • Reduces latency by serving reads from a faster store.
  • Decreases load on origin systems, improving scalability.
  • Enables better user experience for read-heavy workloads.
Common misconception
A cache is not a substitute for correctness—without invalidation it can serve stale data.
Key Takeaway

Use caching to lower latency and origin load, but always pair it with a plan for invalidation and measurable signals like hit rate.

Concrete example
Store session lookups or user profile snippets in an in-memory cache so page renders avoid database joins on each request.
Measure success
Track cache hit rate, origin request rate, and request latency before and after enabling caching.
Fallback behavior
On cache miss, fetch from origin and populate the cache; ensure the fallback path is robust to avoid additional bottlenecks.
Why not always cache?
Writes may be slower, memory is limited, and invalidation adds complexity—cache only what yields meaningful gains.

screens.title: Caching Layers in a Distributed System
screens.narratorSegment: Caching occurs at multiple layers and each layer has distinct latency, freshness, and operational properties. Client-side caches—like a browser cache or mobile app store—are the fastest because they avoid network trips entirely, but they are per-user and limited by device storage and user-controlled settings. CDNs store copies at geographic edges and significantly reduce latency and origin load for static and some dynamic content; they also introduce propagation delays when invalidating edge caches. DNS caching speeds up name resolution but has coarse control via TTLs. Application-level caches, implemented with in-memory stores or dedicated caches such as Redis and Memcached, balance speed and control: they are close to the application and can be tuned for TTL, eviction policies, and clustering. Database-level caching includes buffer pools and query caches inside the DB engine and is optimized for block or query-level reuse. When designing, ask where latency matters most, how often data changes, and who can tolerate slight staleness. For example, caching product images at the CDN edge is safe, but caching inventory counts at the edge without careful invalidation can create incorrect user-visible state. A practical rule: prefer the fastest layer that still lets you invalidate or tolerate eventual consistency for the workload. Which layer would you pick when freshness of data is critical but reads are high?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Caching Layers
Common caching layers
Understand latency, control, and failure trade-offs per layer.
Client-side cache
Fastest; per device; great for static assets and short-lived API responses.
CDN edge cache
Low latency across regions; good for static and cacheable dynamic content; invalidation has propagation delays.
DNS cache
Speeds DNS lookups using TTL; coarser control over freshness.
Application-level cache
In-memory caches like Redis reduce load on databases and are tunable for TTL and eviction.
Database-level cache
Buffer pools and query caches speed repeated queries inside the database engine itself.
Example decision
For product images: CDN edge. For inventory counts requiring strong freshness: avoid CDN edge, use application-level cache with event-driven invalidation or skip caching for absolute correctness.
Key Takeaway

Choose the fastest cache layer that still allows acceptable invalidation and consistency for your workload.

Misconception check
Faster layer is not always better if it prevents timely invalidation of data that must be fresh.

screens.title: Cache Invalidation Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Cache invalidation is the process of keeping cached copies consistent with the primary data store. Three common strategies are write-through, write-back, and write-around. Write-through writes data synchronously to both cache and primary store so the cache always reflects the latest state; it simplifies correctness but slows write latency because the write path waits for both operations. Write-back, also known as write-behind, accepts writes to the cache first and flushes them asynchronously to the primary store; this improves write performance but risks data loss if the cache fails before flushing. Write-around bypasses the cache on writes and writes directly to the database; the new value is only loaded into the cache on the next read, which avoids filling the cache with rarely read writes, but can cause higher read latency for the first subsequent read. A concrete example: updating a product price in an e-commerce system. With write-through the cache holds the new price immediately; with write-back a brief window exists where the database lacks the update until flush; with write-around the cache may still serve old data until the next read refreshes it or invalidation occurs. A common interview trap is failing to mention the write latency and failure risks; always state the concrete trade-off and when you would pick each strategy. Which strategy would you recommend for inventory updates that must be correct on every read?

keyIdea.title: Invalidation Choices
keyIdea.text: Choose write-through for consistency, write-back for write performance, and write-around to avoid caching cold writes—each has clear trade-offs to explain.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Invalidation Strategies
Invalidation Strategies
Trade correctness, latency, and risk across three write strategies.
Write-Through
Writes update both cache and primary store synchronously. Consistent cache state, slower writes.
Write-Back
Writes update cache first and flush to primary asynchronously. Faster writes, possible data loss on cache failure.
Write-Around
Writes go to primary only; cache populated on next read. Avoids filling cache with rare writes but risks an initial slow read.
Concrete scenario
For inventory where absolute freshness matters choose write-through or immediate invalidation; for analytics metrics write-back may be acceptable.
Common pitfall
Picking a strategy without considering failure modes: write-back without durability guarantees risks data loss on cache crash.
Key Takeaway

State the required freshness and write latency constraints, then pick the invalidation strategy whose trade-offs match those constraints.

screens.title: Eviction Policies: LRU, LFU, FIFO, and Random
screens.narratorSegment: Eviction policies decide which items to remove when a cache reaches capacity. The most common is Least Recently Used, or LRU, which evicts the item that has not been accessed for the longest time. LRU assumes temporal locality: recently accessed items are likely to be requested again. Least Frequently Used, LFU, tracks access counts and evicts items with the lowest frequency; it captures long-term popularity but requires maintaining counters. FIFO, first-in first-out, evicts the oldest inserted item regardless of access pattern and is simple but often suboptimal. Random replacement removes a random entry and is easy to implement but usually performs worse than LRU for real workloads. A concrete example: a news feed where trending stories stay hot—LFU may be better; a user session cache with recency-based reuse—LRU fits well. A common misconception is conflating recency and frequency: a frequently accessed item may still be evicted by LRU if it hasn’t been accessed recently. Another design nuance is the cost of bookkeeping: LFU counters and LRU lists have overhead that may affect insert and update latency. Always justify your eviction policy by describing the workload's access distribution and the operational cost of tracking metadata. If access patterns change over time, consider hybrid approaches or TTLs to adapt.

keyIdea.title: Eviction Rules
keyIdea.text: Pick eviction by access pattern: LRU for recency, LFU for long-term popularity, FIFO for simplicity, and avoid random unless simplicity outweighs efficiency.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Eviction Policies
Eviction Policies Explained
Which entries to evict when memory is full—and why.
Least Recently Used (LRU)
Evicts the least recently accessed item—good when recency predicts future access.
Least Frequently Used (LFU)
Evicts items with the fewest accesses—tracks long-term popularity via counters.
First-In, First-Out (FIFO)
Removes the oldest entry by insertion time; simple but may evict hot items.
Random Replacement
Evicts a random item; trivial to implement but often inefficient compared to LRU/LFU.
Example: session cache
Use LRU when recent activity drives reuse.
Example: trending content
LFU fits workloads where long-term popularity matters.
Cost trade-off
LFU bookkeeping is heavier than LRU; justify overhead when access patterns require it.

screens.title: Implementing an LRU Cache (Python)
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing a basic LRU cache clarifies how recency is tracked in practice. The provided implementation uses an ordered dictionary to keep items in access order. On get, if the key exists we pop and reinsert it so it becomes most recently used; on put, if the key already exists we update and move it to the end, otherwise when at capacity we pop the first item which is the least recently used. A concrete walkthrough: initialize the cache with a fixed capacity, call put to add two items, access one with get to mark it as recently used, then insert a third to cause eviction of the least recently used. A common misunderstanding is forgetting to update recency on get—if you only update recency on put you will evict items that are still frequently read. Also be careful with concurrency: a simple single-process OrderedDict implementation is fine for interview questions, but in production you would need synchronization or a distributed cache like Redis with LRU configured. The code example in the content shows a minimal, correct approach and the example usage demonstrates expected outputs. After reading the code, ask yourself how you would extend it to support TTL or thread safety.

keyIdea.title: LRU in Practice
keyIdea.text: Track recency on both get and put; when capacity is reached remove the least recently used entry and preserve access order.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › LRU Implementation
LRU Cache — Starter Code
A compact implementation using OrderedDict for access ordering.
Code
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
  def __init__(self, capacity: int):
    self.cache = OrderedDict()
    self.capacity = capacity

  def get(self, key: int) -> int:
    if key not in self.cache:
      return -1
    # Move the accessed item to the end to mark it as most recently used
    value = self.cache.pop(key)
    self.cache[key] = value
    return value

  def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
    if key in self.cache:
      # If key exists, update its value and move to end
      self.cache.pop(key)
    elif len(self.cache) >= self.capacity:
      # If cache is full, evict the least recently used item (first item)
      self.cache.popitem(last=False)
    # Add the new item (or updated item) to the end
    self.cache[key] = value

# Example Usage:
cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put(1, 1)
cache.put(2, 2)
print(f"Get(1): {cache.get(1)}")    # returns 1
cache.put(3, 3)                     # evicts key 2
print(f"Get(2): {cache.get(2)}")    # returns -1 (not found)
cache.put(4, 4)                     # evicts key 1
print(f"Get(1): {cache.get(1)}")    # returns -1 (not found)
print(f"Get(3): {cache.get(3)}")    # returns 3
print(f"Get(4): {cache.get(4)}")    # returns 4
Explanation & Example
The example usage shows the movement of items to the most-recently-used end and eviction of the least recently used entry when capacity is reached.
Common mistake
Not updating recency on get will degrade LRU behavior and evict active items.
Key Takeaway

LRU requires updating order on both get and put; for production add thread-safety or use a distributed cache for scale.

screens.title: Cache Stampede and Mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: A cache stampede, sometimes called the thundering herd, happens when a highly popular cached item expires and many concurrent requests all miss the cache and hit the origin at once. The origin—often a database—can become overwhelmed, causing spikes in latency or even outages. Concrete mitigation patterns include: using distributed locks or mutexes so that only one process rebuilds the cache while others wait or serve stale data; probabilistic early expiration, which staggers expirations across clients so the cache is refreshed before everyone misses at the exact same time; and using stale-while-revalidate where stale data is served immediately while a background refresh updates the cache. Another tactic is to pre-warm or proactively refresh hot keys before they expire. A common misconception is thinking that short TTLs prevent stale data and always prevent stampedes; short TTLs can increase origin traffic if many clients repeatedly miss. In design discussions, explain trade-offs: locks introduce latency for waiting clients, probabilistic methods may serve slightly stale data but smooth traffic, and stale-while-revalidate prioritizes availability over absolute freshness. Ask yourself which of these mitigations best fits an A P I that must remain highly available under spike conditions.

keyIdea.text: Prevent origin overload by ensuring only limited requests rebuild a hot cache entry—use locks, probabilistic expiry, stale-while-revalidate, or pre-warming.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Cache Stampede
Cache Stampede
Many concurrent cache misses overwhelm the origin—mitigate with locking or smoothing techniques.
Why it happens
A hot key expires and many clients simultaneously request it, causing a surge of origin queries.
Mitigation patterns
  • Distributed mutex so only one rebuilds the cache.
  • Probabilistic early expiration to stagger refreshes.
  • Stale-while-revalidate: serve stale data while background refresh occurs.
  • Pre-warm hot keys proactively.
Concrete example
When a product page goes viral, a single cache expiry can send thousands of requests to the database. Use a distributed lock or serve stale content while one process refreshes the cache.
Key Takeaway

Plan for hot keys: choose a mitigation that balances freshness, availability, and implementation complexity for your service-level goals.

screens.title: TTL, Negative Caching, and Cache Miss Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Time-to-live, or TTL, sets an automatic expiry for cached items so stale data is regularly evicted. For many read-heavy datasets that change infrequently, TTLs are a practical and simple invalidation mechanism. Negative caching extends the idea: cache not-found responses for a short TTL so repeated requests for missing resources do not hammer the origin. Handling cache misses gracefully is essential: on a miss your application must fetch from the primary data source and populate the cache, but it must also avoid cascading failures. For example, if a downstream database is slow, the cache miss path can time out and lead to degraded user experience; consider circuit breaking or rate-limiting origin requests to protect the backend. A common misconception is assuming TTL eliminates all staleness risk. TTLs trade potential staleness for simplicity—shorter TTLs reduce staleness but increase origin load; longer TTLs do the opposite. Choose TTLs based on how quickly data changes and how tolerant clients are to slightly stale values. Finally, document and monitor miss rates and TTL expirations so you can tune these values empirically. What TTL would you choose for product metadata versus session tokens?

Bound staleness with TTLs and cache misses with negative caching and robust fallbacks.
Time-To-Live (TTL)
Automatically expire items after a set duration. Short TTLs mean fresher data and more origin traffic; long TTLs reduce origin load but risk staleness.
Negative caching
Cache not-found responses for a short TTL to avoid repeated origin lookups for missing keys.
Example choices
Product metadata might have moderate TTLs; session tokens may need short TTLs or immediate invalidation on logout for security.

screens.title: Deployment Models and Durability Risks
screens.narratorSegment: When moving beyond a single-process cache you must consider deployment models and durability. Popular in-memory stores used at application-level include Redis and Memcached; both can be deployed standalone or in clustered configurations. Standalone caches are simple but introduce a single point of failure unless clients handle misses gracefully. Clustered or replicated deployments improve availability but add consistency and synchronization concerns. Write-back strategies amplify durability risks: if writes are acknowledged by the cache before flushing to the primary store, failure of the cache can result in lost updates. Mitigations include using persistence on the cache nodes, synchronous replication to multiple cache nodes, or choosing write-through for critical data. Another important production consideration is capacity planning and sharding: partition keys across cache nodes to balance memory and latency. A common interview-level question is to explain how your cache choice affects recovery after failure—describe how you would rehydrate caches, whether you can rebuild from the primary store, and how to avoid thundering herd on cold starts. In short, state the deployment model, the durability guarantees you need, and how you will handle node failures and data rehydration.

Deployment Models & Durability
Standalone vs clustered caches, sharding, and the durability risks of deferred writes.
Standalone cache
Simple to operate but a single point of failure; clients must handle misses and rebuilds.
Clustered/replicated cache
Improves availability but requires coordination, replication configuration, and consistent hashing for sharding.
Write-back durability risk
If a cache acknowledges writes before persistence, a crash can lose updates. Mitigate with persistence or synchronous replication, or choose write-through for critical data.

screens.title: When to Cache and When Not To
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding whether to cache an item requires reasoning about its read:write ratio, change frequency, sensitivity, and the performance benefit. Cache items that are read often and change infrequently—these yield high hit rates and clear performance gains. Avoid caching highly volatile data that must be strongly consistent on every read, such as real-time financial balances, unless you have a robust invalidation and consistency mechanism. Sensitive personal data requires careful handling: encrypt, scope access, or avoid caching if the risk of exposure is unacceptable. Over-caching is another common mistake: caching too many items increases memory use and complicates eviction, sometimes reducing overall efficiency. Also consider the cost of populating the cache on misses; if misses are extremely expensive, ensure your miss handling is robust and consider pre-warming important keys. A practical guideline: measure the expected reduction in origin load and latency versus the cost of invalidation and extra memory. In interviews, present a simple rule-of-thumb: cache when read throughput is high, freshness requirements are moderate, and the cost of a miss is significant. Can you describe a dataset in your experience that should not be cached and why?

keyIdea.text: Cache when reads dominate, change frequency is low, and sensitivity is manageable; avoid caching highly volatile or sensitive data without strong invalidation.

content.html:

When to Cache and When Not To
Balance read benefits against change rate, sensitivity, and maintenance cost.
Cache if
High read volume, low change frequency, and non-sensitive data.
Avoid if
Data must be fresh on every read or contains sensitive user details without strict controls.
Operational note
Over-caching increases memory use and invalidation complexity; measure before you expand cache scope.
Key Takeaway

Apply a cost-benefit rule: cache when the read performance gain outweighs the complexity and risk introduced by caching.

screens.title: Common Caching Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Engineers commonly fall into a few caching pitfalls that can be avoided with deliberate design. Stale data is the most frequent issue—if the origin changes and the cache is not invalidated, users see outdated values. Avoid it by using TTLs for tolerable staleness windows, event-driven invalidation for active updates, or write-through to keep cache and primary store synchronized. Over-caching happens when teams cache everything: it increases memory consumption and complicates invalidation. Cache only the items that yield measurable performance gains. Not handling cache misses gracefully is another problem; always ensure the fallback path to origin is resilient and does not create new bottlenecks. Cache stampede is a peak-load failure mode discussed earlier—mitigate with locks, probabilistic expiry, or serving stale data while refreshing. Security mistakes include caching sensitive data in shared caches without encryption or access controls. Finally, monitoring gaps make it hard to detect problems: track hit rate, miss rate, origin request rate, and latency so you can spot regressions. The practical approach is to define policies before deploying: clear TTLs, invalidation paths, monitoring dashboards, and an incident plan for cache-induced failures.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the essential terms to recall quickly. A cache is temporary storage for frequently accessed data to reduce latency. A cache hit occurs when requested data is found in cache; a miss when it is not and must be fetched from the origin. Time-to-live limits how long items remain in cache automatically. Cache invalidation is the process of keeping cached items consistent with the primary store. Write-through writes to both cache and primary synchronously, write-back defers writes to the primary, and write-around bypasses the cache on writes. Eviction policies decide which items leave when space is needed: LRU evicts the least recently used, LFU evicts the least frequently used, and FIFO evicts the oldest inserted item. Finally, cache stampede is when many clients miss a hot entry simultaneously and overwhelm the origin. Keep these phrases precise and pair each with a short note about when it's appropriate or risky.

fullNarratorScript:
Caching is a simple idea with deep impact: keep frequently used data closer so requests cost less time and backend resources. In this chapter you will learn why caching reduces latency and backend load, the common places it’s applied—from the user's device to a database buffer pool—and the trade-offs that come with consistency and capacity limits. We will ground the ideas with concrete strategies you’ll see in interviews: write-through, write-back, and write-around, and we’ll step through popular eviction policies like LRU, LFU, and FIFO so you can justify design choices. You will also see common pitfalls engineers face: stale data causing incorrect user experience, cache stampedes that overwhelm origins, and over-caching that wastes memory and complicates invalidation. By the end, you’ll be able to describe when to cache, which layer to choose, how to invalidate safely, and how to reason about eviction under capacity constraints. Keep an eye on practical examples: an e-commerce inventory update, a CDN serving static assets, and an in-memory LRU used by an A P I. These examples will let you connect the principles to interview scenarios and real-world trade-offs. Ready to explore the three key areas: layers, invalidation strategies, and eviction policies?

These learning objectives focus your practice on explanation and application. First, you will explain the fundamental principle of caching: why keeping frequently accessed data closer reduces latency and scales systems. You should be able to give a live example such as client-side caching of static assets or an in-memory store reducing database load. Second, you will identify caching layers across a distributed system: client, CDN, DNS, application, and database-level caches, and reason about the latency and failure modes for each. Third, you will describe cache invalidation strategies—write-through, write-back, and write-around—explain their trade-offs for write latency and consistency, and give an interview-worthy recommendation for a given scenario. Fourth, you will understand eviction policies like LRU, LFU, and FIFO, explain when to use each, and how TTL interacts with eviction. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can show competency: describing a strategy for a price update in an e-commerce system, and explaining a mitigation for cache stampede. Keep these skills in mind as you read; they map directly to common interview prompts and real-world constraints.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical milestones you can demonstrate in an interview or design discussion. One milestone is drafting a cache invalidation plan for an e-commerce product update: describe how the update triggers an event that invalidates or updates cache entries to avoid stale prices. Another is choosing an eviction policy for a limited-memory cache: when access is skewed toward recent reads pick LRU, when popularity over time matters prefer LFU, and when simplicity is primary choose FIFO. A third milestone is proposing a mitigation for cache stampede—explain using a distributed mutex or probabilistic early expiration so a single request rebuilds a hot cache entry. The fourth milestone is safe caching of sensitive data: outline when not to cache, and when to encrypt or restrict access. Each milestone asks you to explain the trade-off: faster reads versus more complex writes or potential data loss. Practice describing both benefits and pitfalls concisely; interviewers expect clear recommendations with the reasons and a known downside.

A cache is a temporary storage area that holds frequently accessed data so future requests can be served faster. The central claim is that by keeping a copy of hot data in a faster, closer store you reduce both latency and load on slower origins. Picture a busy library where the closet with seldom-used books is far away; placing the most commonly referenced books on a nearby desk is like caching. The immediate benefit is lower response time for reads and reduced queries to the origin database or remote A P I. That improves scalability: fewer expensive operations means your backend can serve more users. A concrete example is storing rendered user session data in an in-memory cache so page loads skip repeated database queries. A common misconception is that caches always give fresh data; they don’t—unless you design invalidation. Stale caches can return outdated information, and over-reliance on caching can mask correctness bugs. Key practical signals to watch are cache hit rate and the origin request rate. High hit rate with low origin traffic shows successful caching; low hit rate suggests wasted memory or poor key design. As a takeaway, always pair caching with a clear invalidation or TTL strategy and measure hit rates so you know whether the cache is actually helping. How would you measure success for a newly deployed cache in production?

Caching occurs at multiple layers and each layer has distinct latency, freshness, and operational properties. Client-side caches—like a browser cache or mobile app store—are the fastest because they avoid network trips entirely, but they are per-user and limited by device storage and user-controlled settings. CDNs store copies at geographic edges and significantly reduce latency and origin load for static and some dynamic content; they also introduce propagation delays when invalidating edge caches. DNS caching speeds up name resolution but has coarse control via TTLs. Application-level caches, implemented with in-memory stores or dedicated caches such as Redis and Memcached, balance speed and control: they are close to the application and can be tuned for TTL, eviction policies, and clustering. Database-level caching includes buffer pools and query caches inside the DB engine and is optimized for block or query-level reuse. When designing, ask where latency matters most, how often data changes, and who can tolerate slight staleness. For example, caching product images at the CDN edge is safe, but caching inventory counts at the edge without careful invalidation can create incorrect user-visible state. A practical rule: prefer the fastest layer that still lets you invalidate or tolerate eventual consistency for the workload. Which layer would you pick when freshness of data is critical but reads are high?

Cache invalidation is the process of keeping cached copies consistent with the primary data store. Three common strategies are write-through, write-back, and write-around. Write-through writes data synchronously to both cache and primary store so the cache always reflects the latest state; it simplifies correctness but slows write latency because the write path waits for both operations. Write-back, also known as write-behind, accepts writes to the cache first and flushes them asynchronously to the primary store; this improves write performance but risks data loss if the cache fails before flushing. Write-around bypasses the cache on writes and writes directly to the database; the new value is only loaded into the cache on the next read, which avoids filling the cache with rarely read writes, but can cause higher read latency for the first subsequent read. A concrete example: updating a product price in an e-commerce system. With write-through the cache holds the new price immediately; with write-back a brief window exists where the database lacks the update until flush; with write-around the cache may still serve old data until the next read refreshes it or invalidation occurs. A common interview trap is failing to mention the write latency and failure risks; always state the concrete trade-off and when you would pick each strategy. Which strategy would you recommend for inventory updates that must be correct on every read?

Eviction policies decide which items to remove when a cache reaches capacity. The most common is Least Recently Used, or LRU, which evicts the item that has not been accessed for the longest time. LRU assumes temporal locality: recently accessed items are likely to be requested again. Least Frequently Used, LFU, tracks access counts and evicts items with the lowest frequency; it captures long-term popularity but requires maintaining counters. FIFO, first-in first-out, evicts the oldest inserted item regardless of access pattern and is simple but often suboptimal. Random replacement removes a random entry and is easy to implement but usually performs worse than LRU for real workloads. A concrete example: a news feed where trending stories stay hot—LFU may be better; a user session cache with recency-based reuse—LRU fits well. A common misconception is conflating recency and frequency: a frequently accessed item may still be evicted by LRU if it hasn’t been accessed recently. Another design nuance is the cost of bookkeeping: LFU counters and LRU lists have overhead that may affect insert and update latency. Always justify your eviction policy by describing the workload's access distribution and the operational cost of tracking metadata. If access patterns change over time, consider hybrid approaches or TTLs to adapt.

Implementing a basic LRU cache clarifies how recency is tracked in practice. The provided implementation uses an ordered dictionary to keep items in access order. On get, if the key exists we pop and reinsert it so it becomes most recently used; on put, if the key already exists we update and move it to the end, otherwise when at capacity we pop the first item which is the least recently used. A concrete walkthrough: initialize the cache with a fixed capacity, call put to add two items, access one with get to mark it as recently used, then insert a third to cause eviction of the least recently used. A common misunderstanding is forgetting to update recency on get—if you only update recency on put you will evict items that are still frequently read. Also be careful with concurrency: a simple single-process OrderedDict implementation is fine for interview questions, but in production you would need synchronization or a distributed cache like Redis with LRU configured. The code example in the content shows a minimal, correct approach and the example usage demonstrates expected outputs. After reading the code, ask yourself how you would extend it to support TTL or thread safety.

A cache stampede, sometimes called the thundering herd, happens when a highly popular cached item expires and many concurrent requests all miss the cache and hit the origin at once. The origin—often a database—can become overwhelmed, causing spikes in latency or even outages. Concrete mitigation patterns include: using distributed locks or mutexes so that only one process rebuilds the cache while others wait or serve stale data; probabilistic early expiration, which staggers expirations across clients so the cache is refreshed before everyone misses at the exact same time; and using stale-while-revalidate where stale data is served immediately while a background refresh updates the cache. Another tactic is to pre-warm or proactively refresh hot keys before they expire. A common misconception is thinking that short TTLs prevent stale data and always prevent stampedes; short TTLs can increase origin traffic if many clients repeatedly miss. In design discussions, explain trade-offs: locks introduce latency for waiting clients, probabilistic methods may serve slightly stale data but smooth traffic, and stale-while-revalidate prioritizes availability over absolute freshness. Ask yourself which of these mitigations best fits an A P I that must remain highly available under spike conditions.

TTLs trade potential staleness for simplicity—shorter TTLs reduce staleness but increase origin load; longer TTLs do the opposite. Choose TTLs based on how quickly data changes and how tolerant clients are to slightly stale values. Finally, document and monitor miss rates and TTL expirations so you can tune these values empirically. What TTL would you choose for product metadata versus session tokens?

Engineers commonly fall into a few caching pitfalls that can be avoided with deliberate design. Stale data is the most frequent issue—if the origin changes and the cache is not invalidated, users see outdated values. Avoid it by using TTLs for tolerable staleness windows, event-driven invalidation for active updates, or write-through to keep cache and primary store synchronized. Over-caching happens when teams cache everything: it increases memory consumption and complicates invalidation. Cache only the items that yield measurable performance gains. Not handling cache misses gracefully is another problem; always ensure the fallback path to origin is resilient and does not create new bottlenecks. Cache stampede is a peak-load failure mode discussed earlier—mitigate with locks, probabilistic expiry, or serving stale data while refreshing. Security mistakes include caching sensitive data in shared caches without encryption or access controls. Finally, monitoring gaps make it hard to detect problems: track hit rate, miss rate, origin request rate, and latency so you can spot regressions. The practical approach is to define policies before deploying: clear TTLs, invalidation paths, monitoring dashboards, and an incident plan for cache-induced failures.

These are the essential terms to recall quickly. A cache is temporary storage for frequently accessed data to reduce latency. A cache hit occurs when requested data is found in cache; a miss when it is not and must be fetched from the origin. Time-to-live limits how long items remain in cache automatically. Cache invalidation is the process of keeping cached items consistent with the primary store. Write-through writes to both cache and primary synchronously, write-back defers writes to the primary, and write-around bypasses the cache on writes. Eviction policies decide which items leave when space is needed: LRU evicts the least recently used, LFU evicts the least frequently used, and FIFO evicts the oldest inserted item. Finally, cache stampede is when many clients miss a hot entry simultaneously and overwhelm the origin. Keep these phrases precise and pair each with a short note about when it's appropriate or risky.

Here are three short cards to use as anchors when explaining caching in interviews. First, cache selection: choose the cache layer closest to the consumer that still allows acceptable invalidation and freshness. Second, invalidation strategy: name the trade-off clearly—write-through for consistency, write-back for write performance but with durability risk, write-around to avoid caching cold writes. Third, eviction policy: match the policy to workload—LRU for recency, LFU for long-term popularity, FIFO for simplicity; always mention bookkeeping costs and TTL interactions. Use these three anchors to structure short, persuasive answers: state the requirement, pick a layer and invalidation strategy, pick an eviction policy, and call out a mitigation for stampedes or durability risks. This pattern shows interviewers you can translate principles into actionable designs. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
